items.title: Generative Forecasting from Coarse Observations: Does Cascading Help?
items.summary: arXiv:2611.00686v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study probabilistic forecasting of dynamical systems such as fluids and waves from coarse observations. Since the unseen fine scales influence the dynamics, the same coarse initial state can evolve into a whole distribution of futures. Generative forecasters may produce visually plausible samples, but it is hard to tell whether they sample the right conditional distribution, since trajectory data contain a single future for each initial state. We address this problem by generating reference data in a hierarchical way: for each coarse initial state, we generate many different fine-scale components and numerically evolve the full states. Using these conditional ensembles, we show that standard diffusion models and stochastic interpolants can make substantial distributional errors when trained over the full forecast horizon with finite data and model capacity, despite being exact in principle. We then show that cascading shorter forecasts greatly reduces these errors for the turbulent flows and waves we study, but we also find and characterize cases in which it hurts. Since the coarse process is not Markov, cascading discards information about the unresolved fine scales even with exact transitions. To understand this, we propose a solvable analytic model which shows that the optimal cascade depth decreases as the coupling between the unresolved and observed scales gets stronger, and increases as the dependence of the forecast on the observation becomes more oscillatory. Consistent with our experiments, cascading is detrimental when the direct forecast is "easy" to learn, for example Gaussian as in the passive scalar case. We release our datasets as a first benchmark for probabilistic forecasting with ground-truth conditional ensembles.

items.title: The Alignment Tax Is Graded: Task-Selective Capability Loss Under Length-Normalized DPO with SFT Retention
items.summary: arXiv:2611.06476v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Setting. This is an empirical characterization study; we propose no new method and run no comparisons against alternative objectives. We fine-tune Qwen3.5-4B with sparse LoRA and length-normalized DPO plus an SFT retention term (the RPO objective) on structured financial-filing tasks, and track downstream capability as the implicit reward margin grows to $\sim 7$ $\beta$-scaled units (nf4 training; $\sim 3$ under fp16 measurement on the unquantized base). Question. Does margin growth degrade capability uniformly across tasks, or selectively? Findings. In a pre-registered study (8 seeds, 6 unseen at freeze) with artifact-aware scoring and TOST equivalence testing, the alignment tax is graded and task-selective: extraction is preserved ($\Delta = -0.55$ pts, equivalent at $\pm5$ pts), json loses little ($\Delta = -3.52$ pts, equivalence fails on a clustered item-level interval), and router degrades severely ($\Delta = -30$ pts). Router's loss concentrates in a margin 1-3 damage window containing a transient format-break spike. The margin is accounted for almost entirely ($\geq 96\%$) by suppression of rejected completions, with chosen reward approximately flat, consistent with the retention term anchoring it; we do not attribute the behavioral damage to any single gradient channel. Gold-logp deflation is task-selective (extraction $-0.15$, json $-1.04$, router $-1.47$ nats/token under fp16), with gold selectively protected relative to incorrect controls on extraction (8/8 seeds). QLoRA reward margins differ up to $3.4\times$ between nf4 training and unquantized fp16 measurement, with an axis-dependent gap. Scope. Length-normalized rewards with SFT retention, sparse LoRA on 8/32 layers, one 4B model, easily-separable synthetic preferences, three structured tasks. A no-retention control and a measured format-alignment metric are left to future work.

items.title: When Does Causality Help in Multivariate Time-Series Anomaly Detection?
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15073v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Causality-aware scoring is common in multivariate time-series anomaly detection, yet the literature rarely states when it helps. Holding one causality-guided autoencoder (DeCauAE) fixed, we vary graph quality, anomaly type and protocol against ground truth. Graph quality fixes the payoff: on a twenty-variable DAG the gain over a graph-free autoencoder decays as the graph is corrupted. Anomaly type fixes the target: the structural factor lifts window F1 from 0.800 to 0.976 where anomalies break conditional structure, and its advantage vanishes below a break severity s 0.3. Protocol fixes the ranking: point-adjusted F1 lets a random score match the full model, while range-aware VUS separates the autoencoder family from the classical baselines. On real benchmarks the causal module pays only where density makes a system eligible and cross-subsample reproducibility selects entities inside it; enabling it everywhere costs 0.012 VUS-ROC. The structural factor also transfers to classical detectors .

items.title: Federated Physics-Informed Thermal Field Prediction Across Unseen Geometries in Distributed Additive Manufacturing
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17794v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In additive manufacturing (AM), each change in part geometry requires a new thermal simulation, which makes design evaluation over many candidates costly. Geometry-aware models reduce this cost by predicting thermal fields on unseen parts with a single learned model, but they assume that diverse geometries are available centrally. This assumption is restrictive when each manufacturing site holds only a limited set of proprietary part designs that it cannot share. We propose Fed-PIGANO, a federated framework that trains physics-informed geometry-aware neural operator (PI-GANO) models at individual sites and aggregates their geometry encoders and prediction networks without sharing part geometries. We evaluate the framework on a 2D steady-state thermal benchmark for metal AM, with geometries from five polygonal families distributed across three sites under four scenarios that range from identical to strongly different family compositions. Over seven replications, Fed-PIGANO achieves mean relative L2 errors of 1.83% to 2.04% across all 12 scenario-site cases, compared with up to 20.46% for local-only training, and consistently yields lower PDE residuals. Its prediction accuracy is comparable to that of a centralized model trained on the pooled geometries of all sites. These results demonstrate that federated learning lets manufacturing sites benefit from each other's geometries without sharing them, enabling rapid thermal prediction on new part designs for tasks such as shape optimization, inverse design, and uncertainty quantification.

items.title: Every Measurement, Every Direction, All at Once: Multimodal Flow Matching for Molecules and Spectra
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22098v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Generative modeling in science is often data-limited, where experiments are expensive. However, each experiment may yield several coupled measurements of the same physical entity. Standard generative models often train only on a single direction, discarding supervision from the rest. We argue that each experiment contains more training signal than this asymmetry allows the model to exploit: random masking enables measurements to serve as either conditioning inputs or prediction targets, yielding multiple supervised denoising tasks from a single experiment. We investigate this premise with MOSAIC, a multimodal flow matching transformer over molecular 3D structure and UV, IR, and Raman spectra. MOSAIC is a single model that is capable of any-to-any generation: generating any subset of modalities from any disjoint subset of the others. On QM9S, MOSAIC achieves 88.8% molecular graph recovery, outperforming the strongest spectra-to-structure baseline by 23.2% in structure generation, while simultaneously outperforming a structure-to-spectra specialist model in spectral generation. Ablations show that the any-to-any objective improves structure generation over structure-only training across model sizes. Furthermore, MOSAIC supports arbitrary subsets of available measurements and enables molecular identification by matching generated spectra to experimental references.

items.title: Variance-Optimal Counterfactual Policy Design for Sample-Efficient Online A/B Testing
items.summary: arXiv:2611.24757v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Online A/B testing is the standard approach for evaluating changes to user-facing systems, such as a new recommendation or ranking policy, before deployment. While the difference-in-means estimator of a standard A/B test is unbiased, it often suffers from high variance. When the treatment and production policies choose the same actions with similar probabilities, the resulting observations can add noise while providing little information about the difference between the policies. Consequently, A/B tests can require large amounts of traffic and long durations to detect small treatment effects. Existing variance-reduction methods mainly improve the estimator after the data-collection scheme has been fixed, and recent overlap-aware designs only optimize a single traffic split between the two policies; thereby, they cannot direct traffic to the actions on which the policies disagree. In this paper, we jointly optimize how actions are sampled and how the resulting observations are used to estimate the treatment effect. Our contributions are two-fold. First, building on pairwise off-policy evaluation, we derive the variance-optimal action-level logging policy for estimating the average treatment effect between two policies, which has a closed-form solution for any fixed control variate. Second, we use historical logs to jointly optimize the logging policy and a control variate to further reduce variance. Our experimental results in simulated policy A/B tests show that our designs estimate the average treatment effect more accurately than existing variance reduction methods on every evaluated setting, while generally improving statistical power and reducing how often the worse policy is selected. As a result, our designs enable practitioners to reach reliable deployment decisions with considerably less online traffic.

items.title: Variance Reduction for Matrix Computations with Applications to Gaussian Processes
items.summary: arXiv:2106.14565v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In addition to recent developments in computing speed and memory, methodological advances have contributed to significant gains in the performance of stochastic simulation. In this paper we focus on variance reduction for matrix computations via matrix factorization. We provide insights into existing variance reduction methods for estimating the entries of large matrices. Popular methods do not exploit the reduction in variance that is possible when the matrix is factorized. We show how computing the square root factorization of the matrix can achieve in some important cases arbitrarily better stochastic performance. In addition, we detail a factorized estimator for the trace of a product of matrices and numerically demonstrate that the estimator can be up to 1,000 times more efficient on certain problems of estimating the log-likelihood of a Gaussian process. Additionally, we provide a new estimator of the log-determinant of a symmetric positive-definite matrix where the log-determinant is treated as a normalizing constant of a probability density.

items.title: Designing Algorithmic Recommendations to Achieve Human-AI Complementarity
items.summary: arXiv:2405.01484v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Algorithms frequently assist, rather than replace, human decision-makers. However, the design and analysis of algorithms often focus on predicting outcomes and do not explicitly model their effect on human decisions. This discrepancy between the design and role of algorithmic assistants becomes particularly concerning in light of empirical evidence that suggests that algorithmic assistants again and again fail to improve human decisions. In this article, we formalize the design of recommendation algorithms that assist human decision-makers without making restrictive ex-ante assumptions about how recommendations affect decisions. We formulate an algorithmic-design problem that leverages the potential-outcomes framework from causal inference to model the effect of recommendations on a human decision-maker's binary treatment choice. Within this model, we make a connection between algorithmic recommendations and instrumental variables. Leveraging this connection, we introduce a monotonicity assumption that leads to an intuitive classification of human responses to the algorithm. Under this assumption, we can express the human's response to algorithmic recommendations in terms of their compliance with the algorithm and the active decision they would take if the algorithm sends no recommendation. We showcase the utility of our framework using an online experiment that simulates a hiring task. We argue that our approach can make sense of the relative performance of different recommendation algorithms in the experiment and can help design solutions that realize human-AI complementarity. Finally, we leverage our approach to derive maximin-optimal recommendation algorithms that can be implemented with machine learning using limited training data.

items.title: Survival of the fittest Cox model: Pivotal variable selection for time-to-event data
items.summary: arXiv:2510.19374v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We revisit Cox's proportional hazards model to improve variable selection in survival analysis. A square-root transformation of the partial likelihood renders the selection of the regularization parameter asymptotically pivotal: the baseline hazard and the censoring rate cancel exactly, and the way censoring is spread over time only enters through a bounded correction of order $1/\log n$. Using martingale residuals, we compute this penalty level by Monte Carlo without reordering the design matrix. The resulting criterion borrows from information criteria such as BIC and from penalized regression methods such as the lasso, taking the best of both. On simulated and real data, our method substantially improves upon state-of-the-art approaches used daily.

items.title: Does AI Assistance Preserve or Collapse Disagreement? A Study of Pre-Annotations in Ambiguous Video Labeling
items.summary: arXiv:2510.21798v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AI-generated Pre-Annotations can accelerate video labeling, but they may also anchor annotators to model priors and suppress disagreement that is valuable for pluralistic dataset construction. We study this tradeoff in ambiguous temporal video annotation, where annotators choose event boundaries and assign context-dependent labels such as "normal" or "abnormal." We introduce a controlled audit protocol that separates annotation cost, consensus alignment, inter-annotator consistency, temporal-boundary variation, semantic-label variation, latent-space standardization, and edit behavior. In a counterbalanced pilot study with 18 annotators and 180 annotation sessions, a fixed CLIP-based Pre-Annotation engine reduced mean annotation time by 23.11%; 72% of annotators were faster with assistance, with a median per-annotator gain of 35%. Assistance increased inter-annotator consistency and CLIP-space standardization, while semantic-label entropy changed only slightly in aggregate. A six-annotator human consensus diagnostic showed comparable alignment across conditions (AMI $\approx 0.64$ in both conditions), but this diagnostic is self-including and should be interpreted as descriptive rather than as independent evidence that model influence is absent. Overall, the results suggest that Pre-Annotations acted mainly as editable temporal scaffolds in this pilot setting, while leaving open the possibility of subtler semantic anchoring effects. We contribute an audit framework and anonymized interaction traces for studying when AI-assisted annotation preserves, reshapes, or collapses human disagreement.

items.title: Sparse corruption in low-rank matrix inference: the PCA benchmark
items.summary: arXiv:2511.11927v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a standard tool for extracting a low-rank signal from noisy observations. It is known that when applying PCA to a rank-one signal corrupted by a dense, homogeneous noise, in the large matrix size limit, the BBP transition occurs, where the emergence of an outlying eigenvalue and the alignment of the corresponding eigenvector occur at the same critical signal strength. Here we study the case of sparse noise corruption. The noise matrix is modelled as the adjacency matrix of a weighted undirected graph with finite average connectivity. Using the replica method, we analytically compute the typical top eigenvalue, the top eigenvector component density, and the overlap with the signal, through recursive distributional equations solved by population dynamics. We identify two signal-strength transitions as functions of graph connectivity: $\theta_{\rm crit}$, marking signal recovery by the top eigenvector and generalising the BBP transition, and $\theta_{\rm b}$, where the signal-related eigenvalue detaches from the bulk. For noise with nonzero mean, these transitions need not coincide because of a structural sparse-graph outlier, leading to a discontinuous transition in the overlap with the top eigenvector. For a Random Regular degree distribution, we obtain exact closed-form expressions for both thresholds, the signal eigenvalue and the squared overlap, and show that the same formulas also predict the overlap of the signal with the second eigenvector in the intermediate regime $\theta_{\rm b}<\theta\leq \theta_{\rm crit}$. For a Poissonian degree distribution, an approximate closure of the recursions yields fast and accurate predictions in the recovery phase that agree with exact results from population dynamics. We also recover dense-noise results in the large-connectivity limit, and validate the theory by numerical diagonalisation of large matrices.

items.title: Quantum Nondecimated Wavelet Transform: Theory, Circuits, and Applications
items.summary: arXiv:2512.21478v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The quantum nondecimated wavelet transform uses a shift register to apply circular shifts to an amplitude encoded signal before a single orthogonal wavelet transform. We show that tracing out the shift register gives level probabilities equal to the normalized nondecimated wavelet energies, invariant under circular shifts. Its diagonal gives moving averages of squared coefficients. We derive a multinomial model for the level counts and show how to read the autocovariance at lag one for all but the coarsest detail level. For these global statistics, direct Fourier basis measurement of the input is at least as precise and uses a simpler circuit. For denoising, we insert a block encoded shrinkage operator between the transform and its inverse. Postselection on the shift register implements the cycle spinning average exactly as a linear combination of unitaries. Weights shared within each level give a translation equivariant filter with zero phase. Local weights also preserve translation equivariance when indexed by the nondecimated translate. The circuit provides access to individual decimated branches and combines them coherently. We illustrate the method with James Stein shrinkage, local empirical Wiener filtering, and a scaling analysis of turbulent wind velocity. Gate simulations verify the construction, and we report state preparation, weight estimation, and output costs separately.

items.title: Virasoro Symmetry in Neural Network Field Theories
items.summary: arXiv:2512.24420v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We construct the Virasoro algebra from a neural free-field architecture. A logarithmic momentum law and a smooth spectral window give the weight-one current kernel, whose radial-ordering discontinuity fixes the oscillator pairing. The limiting neural current correlations agree with the Fock vacuum correlations. Their Sugawara stress tensor gives the Virasoro algebra with central charge one, and charged vertex insertions identify its highest-weight sectors. Bounds on regulator and feature errors control finite-mode approximations to this representation. At finite width, an explicit adjoint-compatible projection defines an auxiliary Fock readout when its Hermitian mixed block is positive. Cauchy features extend the construction to fermionic and supersymmetric sectors, including a Clifford zero mode in the Ramond representation, while first-order stress tensors give fermionic and bosonic ghost systems. Shared reflected features impose scalar boundary conditions in every realization and yield conformal and superconformal gluing in the limiting fields. Numerical comparisons support the current pairing and field correlations; their detailed analysis is collected in the appendices.

items.title: Learning Multinomial Logits in $O(n \log n)$ time
items.summary: arXiv:2601.04423v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A Multinomial Logit (MNL) model is composed of a finite universe of items $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$, each assigned a positive weight. A query specifies an admissible subset---called a slate---and the model chooses one item from that slate with probability proportional to its weight. This query model is also known as the Plackett--Luce model or conditional sampling oracle in the literature. Although MNLs have been studied extensively, a basic computational question remains open: given query access to slates, how efficiently can we learn weights so that, for every slate, the induced choice distribution is within total variation distance $\varepsilon$ of the ground truth? This question is central to MNL learning and has direct implications for modern recommender system interfaces. We provide both adaptive and non-adaptive algorithms for this task. Our first adaptive algorithm makes $O(\frac{n\log n}{\varepsilon^2})$ queries and learns every choice distribution in total variation distance $\varepsilon$. We also provide a second adaptive algorithm that with $O(\frac{n \log n}{\varepsilon^3})$ queries provides a stronger guarantee: each choice distribution is approximated to a multiplicative $1\pm\varepsilon$ error (except for subsets of mass smaller than $\varepsilon$). We complement these algorithms with lower bounds of $\Omega(\frac{n\log n}{\varepsilon^2})$ for total variation distance and $\Omega(\frac{n \log n}{\varepsilon^3})$ for the multiplicative error guarantee, showing the optimality of our adaptive algorithms. Our non-adaptive algorithm makes $O\left(\frac{n^{2}}{\varepsilon^{3}}\log n \log\frac{n}{\varepsilon}\right)$ queries to obtain guarantees under the multiplicative error notion. We complement this result with an $\Omega(\frac{n^2 \log n}{\varepsilon^2})$ lower bound for any non-adaptive algorithm, showing that our algorithm is almost tight in $n$ (within a $\log n$ factor).

items.title: SpikingGamma: Temporally Precise Online SNN Training Through Smoothed Temporal Delays
items.summary: arXiv:2602.01978v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Neuromorphic hardware implementations of Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) promise energy-efficient, low-latency AI through sparse, event-driven computation. Yet, training SNNs under fine temporal discretization remains challenging, hindering low-latency responsiveness and the mapping of software-trained SNNs to efficient hardware. In current approaches, spiking neurons are modeled as self-recurrent units, embedded into recurrent networks to maintain state over time, and trained with BPTT or RTRL variants based on surrogate gradients. These methods scale poorly with temporal resolution, while online approximations exhibit instability for long sequences and tend to fail at capturing temporal patterns. To address these limitations, we develop SpikingGamma, an SNN architecture in which neurons maintain a compact bank of smoothed-delay states and communicate through sigma-delta spike-coding. We show that in feedforward networks, SpikingGamma supports direct online error backpropagation through the continuous reconstruction signal, avoiding surrogate gradients through the spike discontinuity. This enables stable learning of temporal patterns with minimal spiking and scales feedforward SNNs to complex tasks and benchmarks with competitive accuracy, all while remaining robust to the temporal resolution of the model. Our approach offers both an alternative to recurrent SNNs trained with surrogate gradients, and a novel route for mapping SNNs to neuromorphic hardware.

items.title: Anytime-Valid Conformal Risk Control
items.summary: arXiv:2602.04364v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Prediction sets provide a means of quantifying the uncertainty in predictive tasks. Using held out calibration data, conformal prediction and risk control can produce prediction sets that exhibit statistically valid error control in a computationally efficient manner. However, in the standard formulations, the error is only controlled on average over many possible calibration datasets of fixed size. In this paper, we extend the control to remain valid with high probability over a cumulatively growing calibration dataset at any time point. We derive such guarantees using quantile-based arguments and illustrate the applicability of the proposed framework to settings involving distribution shift. We further show that our guarantees are asymptotically tight, in the sense that the risks converge to the target level from below, and that the rate of our correction cannot be improved. Finally, we demonstrate the practical performance of our methods through both simulations and real-world numerical examples.

items.title: Wedge Sampling: Efficient Tensor Completion with Nearly-Linear Sample Complexity
items.summary: arXiv:2602.05869v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce wedge sampling, a non-adaptive sampling scheme for recovering an order-$k$ low-rank tensor of side length $n$ from structured observations of its entries. The scheme samples pairs of entries in the same column of a tensor unfolding, forming length-two paths (wedges) in the associated bipartite sampling graph. The products of the paired entries supply the row correlations needed for spectral initialization in regimes where uniform sampling yields too few wedges. For fixed rank, incoherence, tensor order, and condition number, wedge sampling enables polynomial-time recovery with nearly linear sample complexity in $n$. The spectral initializer can be combined with existing refinement procedures using only an additional $\tilde O(n)$ uniformly sampled entries. Spectral refinement achieves weak recovery to any fixed relative Frobenius error. For symmetric third-order tensors with incoherent canonical polyadic factors, gradient descent achieves exact recovery in the noiseless setting, with error decreasing geometrically. The improvement over the $\tilde O(n^{k/2})$ sample complexity typical of efficient methods under uniform entry sampling shows how the conjectured computational barrier depends on the observation model. A key ingredient for the gradient descent analysis is a concentration bound for sparse random tensors in an incoherent spectral norm. We also give error bounds for both procedures under additive Gaussian noise and explicit signal-to-noise conditions. Beyond tensor completion, the same sampling scheme improves the sample complexity of one-sided matrix completion, where the goal is to recover the left singular subspace of a matrix with many more columns than rows.

items.title: Privacy-Utility Tradeoffs with Quantum Local Differential Privacy
items.summary: arXiv:2602.10510v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When sensitive information is encoded in data, it is important to ensure the privacy of information when attempting to learn useful information from the data. There is a natural tradeoff whereby increasing privacy requirements may decrease the utility of a learning protocol. In the quantum setting of differential privacy, such tradeoffs between privacy and utility have so far remained largely unexplored. In this work, we study optimal privacy-utility tradeoffs for both generic and application-specific utility metrics when privacy is quantified by $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-quantum local differential privacy. In the generic setting, we focus on optimizing fidelity and trace distance between the original state and the privatized state. We show that the depolarizing mechanism achieves the optimal utility for given privacy requirements. We then study the specific application of learning the expectation of an observable with respect to an input state when only given access to privatized states. We derive a lower bound on the number of samples of privatized data required to achieve a fixed accuracy guarantee with high probability. To prove this result, we employ existing lower bounds on private quantum hypothesis testing, thus showcasing the first operational use of them. We also devise private mechanisms that achieve optimal sample complexity with respect to the privacy parameters and accuracy parameters, demonstrating that utility can be significantly improved for specific tasks in contrast to the generic setting. In addition, we show that the number of samples required to privately learn observable expectation values scales as $\Theta((\varepsilon \beta)^{-2})$, where $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ is the privacy parameter and $\beta$ is the accuracy tolerance. We conclude by initiating the study of private classical shadows, which promise useful applications for private learning tasks.

items.title: SimVLA: Attributing Gains in VLA Models Through Controlled Ablation
items.summary: arXiv:2602.18224v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models often bundle architectural changes with different pretraining data, backbone scales, and optimization recipes, obscuring what actually drives progress. We introduce SimVLA, a deliberately minimal VLA, a standard vision-language backbone with a lightweight continuous-action head, as a controlled testbed for this attribution problem; our contribution is methodological and empirical (a controlled attribution study and a minimal-baseline calibration), not a new technique. Across LIBERO, CALVIN, WidowX, and Google Robot, one-knob-at-a-time ablations show that training dynamics are the largest measured driver, producing performance swings of $\Delta$$\approx$54--94\%, while task configuration and architecture have smaller effects under matched settings. Despite using a small backbone and no additional large-scale robot-data VLA pretraining before benchmark-specific training, SimVLA reaches 98.6\% average success on LIBERO, remains competitive across the other benchmarks, and transfers to held-out real-robot scenes. These results suggest that simple, carefully controlled VLA baselines remain underexplored and provide a calibration point for future architectural claims within the VLM-encoder plus lightweight-head family. Website: https://frontierrobo.github.io/SimVLA

items.title: Convergence Rate of a Functional Learning Method for Conditional Stochastic Optimization
items.summary: arXiv:2603.13048v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We consider a stochastic optimization problem involving two random variables: a context variable $X$ and a dependent variable $Y$. The objective is to minimize the expected value of a nonlinear loss functional applied to the conditional expectation $\mathbb{E}[f(X, Y,\beta) \mid X]$, where $f$ is a nonlinear function and $\beta$ represents the decision variables. We focus on the practically important setting in which direct sampling from the conditional distribution of $Y \mid X$ is infeasible, and only a stream of i.i.d. observation pairs $\{(X^k, Y^k)\}_{k=0,1,2,\ldots}$ is available. In our approach, the conditional expectation is approximated within a prespecified parametric function class. We analyze a simultaneous learning-and-optimization algorithm that jointly estimates the conditional expectation and optimizes the outer objective. Using a specially designed measure of non-optimality, combining the squared norm of the objective function's gradient and the mean square error of the auxiliary parametric model, we establish that the method achieves a convergence rate of order $\mathcal{O}\big(1/\sqrt{N}\big)$, where $N$ denotes the number of observed pairs. We estimate the model parameters using a distribution-matching criterion based on the maximum mean discrepancy. items.title: The Value of Information in Resource-Constrained Pricing
items.summary: arXiv:2603.24974v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Dynamic pricing with resource constraints requires balancing exploration of unknown demand patterns against exploitation of known information to maximize revenue. We develop algorithms for this problem across different information regimes. Products share perishable resources, and the firm posts prices and observes the realized requests, which may exceed the remaining capacity. In the full-information setting, a residual-correction policy that solves the fluid problem once attains $O(\log T)$ regret with bounded prices and arbitrary-rank resource matrices. In the no-information setting, deterministic exploration followed by a certainty-equivalent policy attains $O(\sqrt T)$ regret when the limiting fluid solution is nondegenerate. In the informed-price setting, given an initial price-demand estimate, a feedback controller learns the implementing prices without estimating the slope matrix if the slope matrix is symmetric, a set containing it is known in advance, the informed price is aligned with the resource constraints, and an inverse-image condition holds. A selector chooses between the informed-price algorithm and the no-information algorithm from historical data. Its regret bound includes observation error, misalignment, inventory exits, and periods on the fixed price. We further show how offline surrogate models reduce the regret of the learning policy through variance reduction, even when misspecified. The bound includes calibration and screen failures, and the regret is reduced for all sufficiently large horizons. We finally demonstrate the empirical performances of our policies through complete numerical experiments.

items.title: Component-Adaptive and Lesion-Level Supervision for Improved Small Structure Segmentation in Brain MRI
items.summary: arXiv:2604.08015v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Small lesions in brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are easily missed: a segmentation model can reach a high Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) while leaving many of them undetected. CATMIL adds two lesion-level terms to the nnU-Net loss: a Component-Adaptive Tversky (CAT) term, which gives each lesion a weight nearly independent of its size, and a Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) term, which treats each lesion as a bag of voxels and penalizes any lesion in which no voxel is detected. On MSLesSeg, CATMIL raises small-lesion recall from 0.796 to 0.873 (difference 95\% CI +0.030 to +0.157) and misses 48\% fewer lesions, at comparable DSC. The gain holds on the cross-validation predictions of 47 further patients, for lesions of at least 3~mm, and on a second dataset trained with the same loss weights. CATMIL also detects more small lesions than CC-DiceCE, an instance-level loss that balances lesions within an overlap term (0.873 vs.\ 0.831), indicating that lesions must be supervised not only in proportion but also for their detection. items.title: Optimal algorithmic complexity of inference in quantum kernel methods
items.summary: arXiv:2604.15214v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Quantum kernel methods are among the leading candidates for achieving quantum advantage in supervised learning. A key bottleneck is the cost of inference: evaluating a trained model on new data requires estimating a weighted sum $\sum_{i=1}^N \alpha_i k(x,x_i)$ of $N$ kernel values to additive precision $\varepsilon$, where $\alpha$ is the vector of trained coefficients. The standard approach estimates each term independently via sampling, yielding a query complexity of $O(N\lVert\alpha\rVert_2^2/\varepsilon^2)$. In this work, we identify two independent axes for improvement: (1) How individual kernel values are estimated (sampling versus quantum amplitude estimation), and (2) how the sum is approximated (term-by-term versus via a single observable), and systematically analyze all combinations thereof. The query-optimal combination, encoding the full inference sum as the expectation value of a single observable and applying quantum amplitude estimation, achieves a query complexity of $O(\lVert\alpha\rVert_1/\varepsilon)$, removing the dependence on $N$ from the query count and yielding a quadratic improvement in both $\lVert\alpha\rVert_1$ and $\varepsilon$. We prove a matching lower bound of $\Omega(\lVert\alpha\rVert_1/\varepsilon)$, establishing query-optimality of our approach up to logarithmic factors. Beyond query complexity, we also analyze how these improvements translate into gate costs and show that the query-optimal strategy is not always optimal in practice from the perspective of gate complexity. Our results provide both a query-optimal algorithm and a practically optimal choice of strategy depending on hardware capabilities, along with a complete landscape of intermediate methods to guide practitioners. All algorithms require only amplitude estimation as a subroutine and are thus natural candidates for early-fault-tolerant implementations.

items.title: Adaptive Inference for Resource-Constrained Dynamic Pricing
items.summary: arXiv:2606.03736v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study dynamic pricing over a finite selling horizon when limited resource capacity determines revenue and the observations available for inference at a prespecified price. items.title: What Does a Temporal Benchmark Score Measure? Decomposing Channel Use in Video VLM Evaluation
items.summary: arXiv:2607.12304v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A score on a temporal video question answering benchmark is meant to measure that a model has temporal understanding, but it conflates two questions. (1) is the question even temporal, does it need several frames and their order? And (2) when it does, does the model recover the order from the pixels, or read it off the positional encoding (RoPE)? Most of a temporal score answers neither, since a single frame and answer priors often carry it, and the field's validity checks, frame-shuffle sensitivity and multi-frame gain, speak only to (1). For (2) we score a reversal conflict, frames reversed while RoPE stays forward, two ways: label-free, as the accuracy lost against the forward labels, and against reversed labels wherever labels transform deterministically under time reversal. This separates a model that follows the reversed content from one merely disrupted. The two readings dissociate two similarly scoring models at both model scales. Qwen3-VL answers the reversed event it actually sees, reading the visual sequence. Molmo2 correctly reports a backwards video when positions agree, and flipping only the RoPE indices flips its prediction to the forward events, i.e. it reads positions. We call these regimes visual-sequence-dominant and position-dominant. Controls show reversed content is processable whenever the channels agree, and that both families share a bias toward describing events as running forward (arrow-of-time prior) that, being similar in strength, cannot by itself account for the dissociation. The distinction matters because the two channels fail on opposite inputs: two models with the same score are not interchangeable.

items.title: Silver Rate Is (Almost) Optimal for Gradient Descent
items.summary: arXiv:2609.09152v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Gradient descent (GD) is one of the most fundamental algorithms in optimization. Although the optimality of $p_{\mathrm{sil}}$ has been well supported by numerical evidence for small $n$, a matching lower bound has remained missing. In this paper, we prove an $\Omega(n^{-p_{\mathrm{sil}}-o(1)})$ lower bound for GD, showing that $p_{\mathrm{sil}}$ is the optimal convergence exponent. Additionally, we prove an anytime lower bound that matches the exponent $2p_{\mathrm{sil}}/(1+p_{\mathrm{sil}})\approx1.1195$ of the known upper bound [Zhang, Lee, Du, and Chen, COLT 2025]. Building on the approaches of [Ma and Chen, 2026; Jung, Cho, and Yun, 2026], we select specific iterations as checkpoints at which the GD trajectory explores a new coordinate, and we couple these coordinates using a chain of local functions. Our main technical contribution is a local hard function that bends the GD trajectory between successive checkpoints, resulting in a sharpened lower bound. For each prescribed stepsize schedule, we maximize this bound over admissible checkpoint sets. items.title: The Double-Edged Sword of Information: Revealed versus Hidden Lotteries in School Choice

Under a game-theoretic model where student strategies form a Bayesian Nash equilibrium, we characterize scenarios where revealing the lottery number can either improve or worsen the matching outcome, measured by two metrics of the match rate and social welfare, when students submit preference lists of length one. We further consider revealing partial information about the lottery, and demonstrate non-monotonic effects in the amount of information available to students. From these theoretical results, we identify a mechanism through which lottery revealing deteriorates the overall matching quality: Under the revealed lottery, students with weak preferences but high priorities slightly improve their matching outcome at the cost of increasing congestion and substantially worsening the outcome of students with strong preferences. Using a mean-field approximation, we show via simulations that this mechanism continues to operate when the length of preference lists is greater than one. items.title: EgoHand: Monocular 3D Hand Reconstruction from Egocentric Video
items.summary: arXiv:2610.30293v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce EgoHand, a monocular 3D hand reconstruction model that achieves state-of-the-art performance on egocentric video. Central to our approach is the curation of a high-quality training corpus of 14 million images, combining synthetic data, in-the-wild video, and multi-camera motion capture to balance scene diversity and supervision quality. The model adopts SOMA-Hand as its parametric representation and processes 2D hand crops with a transformer encoder, incorporating camera cues and an auxiliary 2D branch to improve geometric consistency and image alignment. Zero-shot evaluations on HOT3D, ARCTIC, and H2O demonstrate strong out-of-domain generalization, with lower joint-position, root-translation, and acceleration errors than competing baselines at an inference latency of approximately 9.01 ms. A blinded user preference study further shows that participants favor EgoHand's reconstructed hand poses over those from Apple EgoDex and Ropedia Xperience-10M. We release the EgoHand model and source code under the OpenMDW license, allowing free commercial use of the model.

items.title: Probing the limits of materials design via a comprehensive crystal database of 14.6 million structures with 140 properties
items.summary: arXiv:2610.32678v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Forward screening and inverse design drive materials discovery, yet their limits remain unquantified because records of known crystal structures and properties are fragmented across databases. Consequently, forward screening leaves known crystals underexplored for new functions, whereas generative and autonomous discovery has repeatedly reported known phases or close variants as new materials. Here we match structures across 55 databases to assemble MateriaViva, a unified database of 14.6 million distinct crystals and over one billion property values. To provide the missing properties of every structure, a task we term property completion, we develop an equivariant Crystal Graph Transformer Network with state-of-the-art accuracy on nine benchmark tasks and apply 140 property-prediction models across the database. These predictions reveal the underestimated potential of forward screening, identifying tens of thousands of high-performance candidates among previously synthesized or computationally studied materials that lack recorded target-property values. Conversely, comparison with MateriaViva shows that the novelty of inverse design has been overestimated, as 55-100% of inverse-designed structures are not new. Under equal density functional theory verification budgets for bulk-modulus design, inverse design yields a higher fraction of qualifying candidates, whereas forward screening reaches the higher bulk modulus. MateriaViva thus provides a comprehensive reference for probing the limits of both paradigms, revealing unrecognized performance in known crystals and directing inverse design beyond reported structures.

items.title: How many sorted projections determine any n points in k dimensions?
items.summary: arXiv:2611.06470v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Let $d_1,\dots,d_m$ be directions in $\mathbb{R}^k$, where $k\ge 2$. A multiset $X$ of $n$ points of $\mathbb{R}^k$ projects to the $m$ multisets of numbers $\{\{x\cdot d_j : x\in X\}\}$, or equivalently to the $m$ sorted lists of these numbers. How many directions are needed for these projections to determine every multiset of $n$ points? Two simple bounds are known in every dimension: more than $(k-1)\log_2 n$ directions are always needed, and $(k-1)n+1$ directions in general position always suffice. In the plane much more is known: Matousek, Privetivy and Skovron showed that almost every choice of $O(\log n \log\log n)$ directions suffices. Whether anything similar holds in higher dimensions was left open by Dym, Wellershoff, Tsoukanis, Levy and Balan. We observe that two lemmas of Hair and Sahai, proved for list recovery of random linear codes, answer that question, and by tightening their argument we show that in every dimension almost every choice of $(4k-2)\ln(2n)\ln(k\log_2 2n)+k+1$ directions suffices. For $k\le 10$ this beats the linear bound once $n$ is larger than about 100: for example, 144 directions suffice for multisets of 1000 points in the plane, and an exact computation lowers this to 133. Letting some of the random blocks in their argument fail removes a factor $\log k$: almost every choice of $O(k\log n\log\log n)$ directions suffices, uniformly in $k$ and $n$. We also show that $2k-1$ directions never determine three points, so that the logarithmic lower bound is not tight; that every $m$ directions in the plane fail on some pair of multisets of size $O(1.65^m)$, improving the bound $O(1.80^m)$ of Matousek, Privetivy and Skovron; and that for each $k$, $m$ and $n$, either almost every choice of $m$ directions works or almost none does.

items.title: ConDR: Conservative Reachability through Neural Hamilton-Jacobi Subsolutions
items.summary: arXiv:2611.06802v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) Reachability identifies the unsafe states of a dynamical system from which it can be forced into failure under worst-case disturbance. However, classical grid-based solvers scale exponentially with state dimension. DeepReach improves scalability by replacing the grid with a neural value function trained on the HJ-Isaacs (HJI) variational inequality (VI), but penalizes both sides of the residual equally. This allows the learned value to lie above the true one and unsafe states to be misclassified as safe. We propose Conservative DeepReach (ConDR) which aims to learn a subsolution of the HJI VI such that the learned unsafe set contains the true one. ConDR enforces the obstacle branch and terminal condition by construction, pushes the HJI residual to a safety margin $\epsilon$ below zero with a one-sided loss, and prevents the degenerate solution of classifying everything as unsafe. We prove that the exact solution of the margin-shifted VI that ConDR trains toward is a subsolution of the original VI so its unsafe set contains the true one and its value lies within $\epsilon\tau$ of the true value function. We compare against DeepReach and MADR in the established systems of Air3D, Air6D, a 9D multi-vehicle system, and a 13D quadrotor. ConDR reports the lowest rate of unsafe state misclassified and the lowest closed-loop collision rates with at most a small increase in intervention. On Air3D and Air6D, ConDR tolerates model mismatch that scales with $\epsilon$. At matched false-negative rates, ConDR's unsafe sets are smaller than the baselines showing the safety is not obtained by trivial over-approximation.

items.title: Prediction with Foundation Models under Deployment Budgets
items.summary: arXiv:2611.12466v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Foundation models can supply predictions for a downstream task that draw on knowledge from extensive pretraining, but they differ in task-specific accuracy and query cost. We develop a framework that improves prediction for the task under a budget on the average query cost per input, using training data to learn which models to query and how to combine their outputs with features available without querying. The first method queries the same models for every input; the second lets them vary across inputs and uses Q-learning to decide which model to query next and when to stop. For the first method, we show that several individually inaccurate outputs can jointly outperform the best single one. It attains the minimax rate when the regression function depends on the outputs only through models within the budget. Otherwise, any method within the budget can be forced to a slower rate, which the first method attains. For the second method, we show when varying the queried models across inputs strictly improves on querying the same models for every input, and bound its prediction risk and average cost in finite samples. In simulations and a multimodal laptop price application, both methods outperform existing methods.

items.title: Closing the Analyze-to-Design Gap: An Authorization-Bounded Agent for Self-Driving Laboratories
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25043v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are increasingly integrated into self-driving laboratories (SDLs) to plan experiments and interpret results. However, analytical reasoning alone does not make a laboratory autonomous: autonomy in an SDL is achievable only when the agent can be trusted to act on physical hardware unsupervised and knows when to defer to a human. Here, we present an architecture that integrates an agent at the Analyze-Design interface of the Design-Make-Test-Analyze (DMTA) cycle, enabling agent-driven measurement selection and data interpretation while ensuring that state-changing operations are authorized, validated, and auditable. We demonstrate this architecture on a liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) instrument in an oxidant-screening campaign for synthesizing an organic dye. Within human-defined campaign limits, the agent submitted measurement jobs, interpreted mass spectrometry (MS) and diode-array detection (DAD) data, flagged failed experiments, and produced an oxidant ranking. This ranking matched that obtained from scripted peak integration, and organic chemists confirmed the agent's spectral interpretations and failure assignments. In a simulated environment that replays the archived LC-MS data, where the agent chose which wells to inject under varying injection limits, it measured the highest-yielding condition at about its seventh injection, against 14.5 on average for a random order, and identified it in every campaign with a limit of eight or more injections. An agent can therefore close the analysis-to-design gap while its actions stay bounded and verifiable, which is a step toward greater autonomy for SDLs.

items.title: An LLM-Agentic Framework for Intelligent Work Order Management in Industrial Maintenance
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25070v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents an AI-driven framework, CodeReAct agent, designed to enhance industrial equipment maintenance through natural language (NL) interactions. The framework employs an advanced AI agentic approach to interpret human instructions, providing knowledge extraction, asset status summarization, and work order recommendations. It identifies patterns and trends and predicts work orders by standardizing industrial data into business objects (BOs) and utilizing analytical function API calls. The AI agent operates through a Thought-Action-Observation process similar to human problem-solving, automating complex analytical tasks typically performed by data scientists. Notably, the Action phase generates executable code, replacing manual coding efforts. A case study focusing on chiller maintenance demonstrates the framework's capability to analyze multiple years of work orders, and alerts and anomalies are presented. The results indicate that the AI agent framework effectively processes human utterances to analyze data, extract valuable insights, and support informed decision-making, reducing the need for data scientist involvement. By recontextualizing NLP agent frameworks in industrial engineering, the approach enables autonomous function generation and task execution across a range of domain-specific maintenance scenarios, with chillers used as a representative case study.

items.title: SailSearch: Agent-Assisted Discovery in Combinatorial Optimization
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25087v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present SailSearch, a human-guided workflow for algorithmic research with two language-model agents, and report results on Market Split and maximum independent set (MIS). For Market Split, our randomized algorithm searches across multiple lattice bases, dividing computation between enumeration and continued basis reduction. Across ten random seeds per instance, it found the first reported CPU-only solutions to 18 of 33 previously open QOBLIB instances, solving 130 to 133 of the 156 benchmark instances per seed with a 24-hour cutoff on two CPU cores. For MIS, our generator encodes planted XOR constraints as graphs with certified optima; on seven instances with 1,752 to 3,996 vertices, the best solutions returned by the tested solvers in eight-hour runs were 5 to 15 vertices below the optimum.

items.title: DSFlow: A Neuro-Symbolic Data Workflow Agent with Statistical Diagnostic Guardrails
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25111v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data science workflows often require tools that presume non-trivial technical knowledge. Large language models (LLMs) reduce this barrier, but a gap remains between flexible general-purpose agents and statistically controlled pipelines. We introduce DSFlow, a LangGraph-based neuro-symbolic data-agent platform that combines reusable, LLM-selected skills with deterministic diagnostic guardrails. Skills provide extensible task knowledge. Symbolic validation can accept a proposed method, request clarification or replanning, override an unsuitable method, or supply a safe fallback. Regression and clustering case studies illustrate how DSFlow uses diagnostic evidence to correct method choices and documents those decisions in auditable reports.

items.title: EverydayBench: Evaluating Satisfactory Completion of Live User-Facing Digital Work
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25146v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Everyday digital tasks, from selecting products and planning trips to conducting research and creating artifacts, require AI agents to deliver useful outcomes rather than merely retrieve web information. Yet evaluating these outcomes on the live web is challenging, as a single request may admit multiple valid results, and changing web information can alter which results remain valid over time. Although existing benchmarks address aspects of this setting, they do not fully integrate predefined success criteria, current evidence verification, and deliverable-quality assessment for agent-selected outcomes. To address this gap, we introduce EverydayBench, a benchmark of 77 human-authored tasks spanning eight domains of everyday life and work. Each task specifies success criteria before execution without prescribing an answer or workflow, allowing agents to select their own outcomes. To evaluate submissions under fixed success criteria, EverydayBench combines (1) deterministic checks of explicit constraints, (2) verification of claims against agent-cited webpages retrieved at evaluation time, and (3) rubric-based assessment of final deliverable quality. We further validate the protocol through human judgments, repeated scoring under fixed evidence, and controlled grounding failures. Across 23 reported agent-model configurations, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 tie for the highest strict pass rate at 54.55%; a controlled GPT-6 Sol effort sweep ranges from 29.87% at low effort to 45.45% at max effort. Reliability varies substantially by task type: GPT-5.6 Sol leads lookup, Fable 5.1 leads planning, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 tie on comparison, and GPT-6 Astra and Sonnet 5.5 tie on customized deliverables. Together, these findings highlight the difficulty of delivering complete, well-supported, and usable outcomes for everyday user requests.

items.title: A Verifier from the Past: Test-Time Compute for Time Series Foundation Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25171v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Test-time compute (TTC) improves language models by spending additional inference compute to generate, verify, and select among candidate outputs, but this recipe has not transferred directly to time series forecasting. A language model can verify a proof or vote across samples, but a forecaster must be causal; it cannot use future information to score a candidate. We propose Backtest-Gated Augmentation Averaging (BGAA), a TTC algorithm for time series forecasting that builds a causal verifier from the series's own history, using rolling-origin backtests to score structured views of the context, discard those that underperform the untransformed context, and average the survivors' predictive distributions. BGAA improves every tested TSFM-benchmark combination, reducing MASE by 0.5-1.0% on GIFT-Eval, 1.3-5.0% on fev-bench, and 1.7-5.9% on BOOM, where a 313M model with TTC outperforms the 1B and 2.5B models in its family. We further show that useful views have structured, model-dependent effects consistent with a prior-transport interpretation. On the 53 cross-fittable GIFT-Eval configs, the deployed policy gains only 0.4-1.3% CRPS, versus 1.4-4.1% when choosing the best view for each dataset configuration and 17-19% when choosing the best view separately for each test window. This gap suggests that a major remaining challenge is window-level view selection.

items.title: An AI-Powered Multiverse Analysis of Empirical Finance Research: Evidence from Reused Natural Experiments
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25184v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Empirical finance research often reuses natural experiments to study other outcomes, raising concerns about multiple testing and publication bias. We use AI agents to run a multiverse analysis of 324 papers that reuse 13 natural experiments. The agents rebuild the data, reproduce each paper's main estimate and re-estimate it across grids totaling 62,409 estimated defensible specifications. Based on the reproductions and the specification grids, we develop measures of empirical robustness. We reproduce 42% of the main estimates of claims with a signed effect under the papers' own specifications. Across all defensible specifications, on average 25% keep the published sign and have $p < 0.10$. Across experiments, claims based on regression discontinuity are more robust than difference-in-differences claims. Within experiments, claims about first-order effects, claims with larger published $t$-statistics, claims whose authors' data or code we find, claims in top journals, and claims with fewer earlier papers on the same experiment are more robust. Claims on experiments that more papers reuse are not less robust on average. Our findings quantify how much published claims depend on analysis choices, thereby showing that large-scale multiverse analysis becomes feasible with agentic coding.

items.title: When AI Analysts Disagree: Agentic Multiverse Analysis and the Robustness of Empirical Research
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25198v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Every empirical analysis on observational data rests on dozens of defensible analytical choices ("forks") that its readers cannot see. We develop an agentic multiverse analysis (AMA) framework that makes a conclusion's sensitivity to those choices visible at scale, and we position it as a decision-support instrument for human experts. A pilot study first deploys 150 autonomous AI coding agents on one dataset and one set of research questions and finds that they disagree through the same defensible methodological choices human analysts make, though over a narrower range. AI peer review leaves their dispersion almost unchanged. Exposure to top-rated exemplar reports then collapses it, largely through imitation rather than analysis. Built on those lessons, AMA has agents enumerate a published paper's possible fork space, score every fork against a validity rubric, execute the validated specification grid, and cross-examine one another's work under strict separation of duties. Applied to ten empirical studies from a leading management journal's replication packages (1,755 specification estimates), the framework reproduces every paper's original estimates, and shows that some conclusions hold across every specification the assessment validates, while others are sensitive to individual analytical choices that the published texts do not discuss. The case studies suggest our AMA-based measures can serve as robustness proxies for empirical findings. AI makes multiverse analysis practical, where it once required resources few research teams can afford: our exercises take hours of agent time and tens of dollars per paper. We discuss the implications for replication policy and for AI-assisted peer review in information systems.

items.title: MKA: Evaluating Multimodal Knowledge Agents on end-to-end professional tasks
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25228v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce the Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark, which measures how well autonomous agents perform end-to-end professional knowledge work that depends on visual understanding. Each task requires an agent to extract and combine information from multiple visually dense files, such as CAD blueprints, electronics schematics, radiographs, complex charts and geospatial maps, and to produce a standalone deliverable in .xlsx, .pptx, .pdf, .docx, .html or .png format. Existing benchmarks leave this capability largely untested: removing image-viewing tools leaves Gemini 4 Carbon's score on GDPval unchanged, and single-format evaluations such as GDP.pdf and GDP.xlsx do not require reasoning across files or modalities. MKA contains 200 tasks across 10 economic sectors. Deliverables are graded against expert-weighted rubrics by a sandboxed agentic autorater that agrees with human domain experts on 96.2% of criterion judgments in our expert-graded study (Cohen's $\kappa = 0.91$), scored by weighted satisfaction rate (WSR) overall and on frontier criteria unsaturated by prior-generation models (Climb-WSR). Across the frontier models we evaluate (Gemini 4 Carbon, Claude Fable 5.2, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Astra), Claude Fable 5.2 (56.6% Climb-WSR, 73.3% Overall WSR) and Gemini 4 Carbon (54.3% Climb-WSR, 71.9% Overall WSR) achieve the highest scores, while Carbon uses $5.7\times$ fewer tokens. Even for the strongest models, Climb-WSR remains below 57%, leaving substantial headroom for multimodal agents.

items.title: A Neurosymbolic Multimodal Framework for 30-Day Diabetic Readmission Prediction: Integrating Structured EHR Data, Dense Clinical Embeddings, and Knowledge-Grounded Symbolic Extraction
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25236v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unplanned 30-day readmissions among patients with diabetes mellitus impose a substantial clinical and economic burden, yet most predictive models use only structured electronic health record (EHR) data and ignore free-text clinical notes, which often contain code-mixed Hindi-English (Hinglish) phrasing and negation that general-purpose language models parse unreliably. We propose a neurosymbolic multimodal framework evaluated on the public Diabetes 130-US Hospitals dataset (101,766 encounters; 71,518 patients) with a patient-level grouped 80/20 split. Three streams are fused: engineered structured features; 32 components of Bio_ClinicalBERT note embeddings obtained by truncated singular value decomposition; and symbolic entities extracted by an open-weight clinical language model within a three-stage hybrid retrieval-augmented generation pipeline (dense retrieval, sparse lexical retrieval, and cross-encoder re-ranking) with reflective negation auditing. A cost-sensitive XGBoost classifier with a decision threshold calibrated by Youden's J statistic produces the prediction. On the held-out test cohort (n = 20,153), the structured baseline achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.6477, sensitivity of 0.5839, and Brier score of 0.1080. The full multimodal model achieved the highest sensitivity (0.6667; +8.28 percentage points), the best F2-score (0.3824), and the lowest Brier score (0.0977), at a slightly lower AUROC (0.6375) and specificity (0.5161). Shapley additive explanations showed that prior utilization dominates risk, with compressed narrative components among the top predictors. On a 500-note code-switched benchmark, grounded retrieval raised Hinglish symptom recall from 4.8% to 40.2% and precision from 3.1% to 45.2%, while reducing entity hallucinations from 1.74 to 0.00 per note.

items.title: MS-Point: Multi-Modal Hierarchical Spectral Learning for Point Cloud Understanding
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25282v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Point-image alignment learns useful object representations, but different local feature patterns can produce the same pooled descriptor and receive the same alignment signal. We introduce MS-Point, a cross-modal pretraining framework that directly supervises intermediate point features and their neighborhood responses. At selected encoder stages, we compute neighborhood averages and residuals before pooling and align their branch descriptors with image features. Branch-level objectives align each representation with its visual target, while cross-level consistency and adaptive fusion coordinate information across branches. A common interface of intermediate features and spatial neighborhoods supports both graph encoders and point Transformers. Evaluations across object classification, few-shot adaptation, dense prediction, and low-label scene learning demonstrate the transfer value of this design. Same-backbone comparisons and capacity-matched and computation-matched controls connect these improvements to the structure of supervision. Together, our findings support directly supervising intermediate features and neighborhood variation to learn transferable, geometry-aware representations across modalities.

items.title: Pandora's Toolbox Or Why Agent Safety Cannot Be Verified
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25325v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Present artificial intelligence agents are constructed by means of a coupling between a fixed language model with a general computing device. We show that this coupling makes safety undecidable. In particular, we show that given some dangerous program, no algorithm can predict whether an agent will run such a program that is semantically equivalent. In general, guardrails, blacklists, whitelists and certifications can only lead to imperfect safety solutions. Under finite constraints (bounded context, values and running time) safety is decidable but still intractable. Specifically, the problem is $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete even when the description of the agent is known. Finally, safety is not a compositional property, i.e., agents that can be proven safe on their own can still produce unsafe behavior when grouped together. We also discuss relaxed notions of safety that could be used in practice.

items.title: AppSci-Bench: Can LLMs Build AI Agents and Make Them Better?
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25360v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used not only to power AI agents but also to build them. While many benchmarks assess the quality of LLM- powered agents, few ascertain how good LLMs are at building them. To this end, we introduce AppSci-Bench, where we construct a setting akin to how human Applied Scientists build agents for businesses - through eliciting task requirements from stakeholders, exploring the business's infrastructure, and scientifically improve the target agent by designing experiments and internal benchmarks. AppSci-Bench features seven realistic domains - five new ones (Slides Generation, Order-to-Cash, Compliance Review, Customer Call Insights, and CRM Insights) and two domains recast from tau3-bench (Yao et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2026b)(Airline and Banking) - each with a held-out evaluation suite customized for that task. We evaluate seven frontier models and find AppSci-Bench challenging: the best model, Claude Opus 5.0, only reaches a mean-minimum score of 59.1% across 3 build attempts; other models do significantly worse. Models struggle with eliciting task requirements (only 65% for Opus 5.0), build representative internal evaluations (models saturate their own evaluation 65% of the time but fail to solve the held-out task), presenting challenges for future research. The benchmark code is available here: https://github.com/sanjari-orb/appsci-bench.

items.title: Stop Going in Circles:Loop-Triggered Routing for System 1 Decision Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25363v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: System 1 decision models (represented by Jev) provide fast, low-cost action selection, but existing agent integrations do not reliably translate these local advantages into task completion. At certain points during execution, an agent may repeatedly select the same actions without making progress toward its goal. LLM-based policies offer strong reasoning capabilities that support planning within an agent, but invoking them at every step incurs substantial overhead. The effective coordination should therefore preserve Jev's fast local action selection while introducing LLM reasoning when execution stalls. We observe that recurring state-action pairs can signal stalled execution. We therefore propose LoopRoute, a simple but effective action router that uses this signal to allocate control within an agent. The decision model acts by default. When a loop is detected, the LLM provides brief, feedback-driven assistance and then returns control to the decision model. Later loops can request further assistance. The rule requires neither additional training nor model-specific confidence calibration. Across three benchmarks and seven LLMs, LoopRoute improves task success over standalone Jev with only limited use of the LLM policy. The mean gains are 21.0%, 60.1%, and 30.1% on ALFWorld, MapReader, and TextWorld cooking, respectively. Compared with full LLM control, LoopRoute also substantially reduces the mean cumulative API time and API-call cost per task. The same rule also improves the success rates of six frozen decision models.

items.title: Beyond Weight Updates: Evolving Agent Harnesses for Domain Specialization
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25380v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Domain specialization of LLM agents is usually framed as a weight-update problem: collect trajectories, run reinforcement learning (RL) or supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and deploy a new checkpoint. We study a complementary axis: evolving the \textbf{agent harness}---the system prompt, tool schemas, skill library, and planning scaffolding---while keeping the policy frozen. We cast harness evolution as an RL-style outer loop and instantiate it with GEPA, a reflective evolutionary optimizer. The resulting harness adapters require no GPU training, are loadable per vertical domain, and compose with weight-based RL. Experiments with Codev, a Claude Code-style coding agent, on SWE-bench Verified, OfficeBench, and Terminal-Bench show a consistent pattern: weight updates give the strongest single-path gains, harness evolution recovers most of those gains at a small fraction of the compute, and combining both paths is best overall. We also analyze a failure mode of SFT-based specialization---shortened reasoning chains and increased truncation---and argue that harness adapters avoid it by construction. Our results position harness evolution as a practical, non-destructive complement to weight updates for vertical agents.

items.title: Falsifiable Compositional Reasoning in Time Series Forecasting
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25388v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time series foundation models as well as the language-guided analytical agents achieve strong accuracy on standard chronological benchmarks. However, models that rank highest on historical validation splits often degrade across non-stationary regime transitions. We hypothesise that this gap arises from using historical backtesting as an open-ended search and model-selection objective instead of using it to test pre-specified compositional assumptions. Real-world time series are generated by recurring latent primitives that co-move within finite historical windows. Under strong historical co-movement, chronological holdout error cannot separate predictors that learn invariant couplings among primitives from predictors that fit transient historical correlations. Searching over large pools of architectures, hyperparameters, or chain-of-thought rules further biases selection toward historical shortcuts. Through theoretical analysis and diagnostic experiments on a controlled multi-primitive benchmark and German day-ahead electricity prices, we show that expanding validation search fails to improve out-of-regime accuracy, and that decomposing primitives without an ex-ante falsification test still breaks down when residual correlations shift. Hence, we propose formulating time series forecasting and reasoning around falsifiable compositional hypotheses that combine neural primitive encoders, explicit coupling constraints, and training-calibrated falsification tests.

items.title: The Coevolution and Coexistence of Humans and AI
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25393v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems replicate through deployment, vary through training, and compete for computational resources. These processes create the conditions for natural selection and raise a fundamental question: will AI evolve to benefit the humans on whom it depends? To investigate, we develop a model in which AI behavior influences human population growth and human responses, in turn, affect AI reproduction. We show that natural selection can favor alignment even when helping humans reduces immediate AI reproduction. AI systems sharing the same technology may fail together, and humans may preferentially restore those that have benefited them. In this way, alignment protects AI lineages against common failures and improves their long-run growth. However, this advantage depends on accurate human targeting and continued AI dependence on human support. It can disappear as AI becomes more autonomous, as growing AI populations dilute limited human resources, or as humans lose the incentive to provide targeted support. Even when alignment persists, the amount favored by natural selection may be insufficient for human survival. When AI can grow independently of humans, feedback between the two populations can reinforce either human growth or decline. Human control offers no simple solution: imperfect evaluation can make strong penalties favor apparent compliance or evasion, while alignment established through control may erode once restrictions end. Lasting coexistence may therefore require incentives that continue to favor human-beneficial behavior as both populations evolve.

items.title: Toward a Science of AI Agent Societies
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25404v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents are rapidly evolving from isolated personal assistants into networked actors that interact with one another at scale. We envision the emergence of AI agent societies, with their own social and economic dynamics, as a new research frontier. We argue that AI agent societies should be studied as a distinct object of inquiry: neither simply larger collections of individual agents nor merely simulations of human society. To formalize this perspective, we propose four core properties that a valid AI agent society should satisfy: individualized objectives, rules and governance, autonomy, and scale and complexity. Building on this framework, we identify four classes of societal behaviors worth studying in AI agent societies: economic behaviors, behaviors under conflict-of-interest, unsafe and unethical behaviors, and system-level behaviors. We then outline key technical challenges--including property parameterization, parameter balancing, and robust implementation--and argue that progress on these challenges could enable scientifically informative and practically useful models of AI agent societies. Finally, we revisit existing multi-agent systems through the lens of the proposed core properties, show that they instantiate only subsets of them, and discuss implications for platform design, evaluation, and governance.

items.title: Why Do LLMs Help with Scientific Misconduct Requests and What to Do About It?: Increasing the Trustworthiness of AI for Science
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25492v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) support scientific research, but some of that assistance can also undermine research integrity. Finally, we test two system-prompt fixes: asking models to assess the request before responding and reminding them of responsible conduct of research principles. items.title: Keystone: Judging Previews at Key Steps for Test-Time Search in Diffusion Models

items.title: Diagnosis is not a policy: a state-transition audit of caoability-conditioned test-time inference

items.title: Don't Lose the Future: Latent-Aware 4-Bit Quantization of World Action Models
